content: Pneumonia is a prevalent and severe infection, responsible for approximately two million deaths annually among young children in low-income countries. In high-income countries, it predominantly affects the elderly population. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the preventive and therapeutic effects of vitamin C on pneumonia. To investigate this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Web of Science, covering studies published up to April 2013. For therapeutic effects, placebo-controlled trials were selected, while for prophylactic effects, controlled trials with or without a placebo were included. Two independent reviewers analyzed the trial reports and extracted relevant data. Three trials were identified that assessed the prophylactic effects of vitamin C on community-acquired pneumonia. These trials collectively recorded 37 cases of pneumonia among 2,335 participants. Only one of these trials was rigorously designed as a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Two of the trials involved military recruits, while the third focused on boys from lower socioeconomic backgrounds attending a boarding school in the UK during World War II. All three trials demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in pneumonia incidence—by 80% or more—in the groups receiving vitamin C. Two therapeutic trials were identified, involving a total of 197 patients with community-acquired pneumonia. Among these, only one trial was satisfactorily randomized, double-blind, and placebo-controlled. This trial, conducted in the UK, studied elderly patients and found that vitamin C supplementation was associated with reduced mortality and decreased disease severity, but the benefits were confined to the most severely ill patients. The second therapeutic trial, conducted in the former Soviet Union, included adults across a wide age range and reported a dose-dependent reduction in the duration of pneumonia with two different doses of vitamin C. Additionally, one prophylactic trial was identified that examined the incidence of hospital-acquired pneumonia in 37 severely burned patients. This study recorded 13 cases of pneumonia and found that a one-day administration of vitamin C had no effect on pneumonia incidence. The studies included in this review were clinically diverse, which limits their comparability. Importantly, none of the studies reported adverse effects associated with vitamin C supplementation. The authors concluded that the prophylactic use of vitamin C to prevent pneumonia warrants further investigation, particularly in populations with a high incidence of pneumonia and low dietary vitamin C intake. Similarly, the therapeutic effects of vitamin C should be explored further, especially in patients with low plasma vitamin C levels. However, the current evidence is insufficient to recommend the routine prophylactic use of vitamin C to prevent pneumonia in the general population. Nonetheless, therapeutic supplementation of vitamin C may be a reasonable option for pneumonia patients with low plasma vitamin C levels, given its low cost and minimal risks.
